title: TRANSMIT AND RECEIVE KA-BAND DIFFERENTIAL FRONT-END FOR DIRECT RADIATING ARRAY ANTENNAS (ARTES AT 5C.537) - EXPRO+
description: Objective: This objective of the activity is to design, develop and experimentally validate a full-scale engineering model of a transmit and receive differential front-end in Ka-band for direct radiating array antennas for satcom applications, employing differential MMIC amplifiers (power amplifier and low noise amplifier), a differential diplexer, and suitable differential RF transitions.Targeted Improvements: - Size, power and weight reduction by 30%.- Simplified front-end architecture by halving the number of RF lines and reducing number of transitions.- Reduction of common mode noise levels and cross-polarisation isolation by at least 10 dB compared to single-ended solution.Description: The development of differential front-ends for full-duplex in-band communications enables improved RF performance compared to single-ended equivalent, as differential circuits have inherent high-cross polarisation isolation and a higher immunity to noise and electromagnetic interference, which are essential for high-data throughput satcom. By combining the RF active and passive differential development, it becomes possible to co-design MMIC amplifiers and their drivers along with passive devices (such as diplexers and RFtransitions). Therefore, impedance matching at active/passive interfaces can be simplified. Additionally, solid-state power amplifiers in differential-mode operation can achieve better linearity and larger voltage swing. MMIC amplifiers use on-chip combining networks to combine the power of multiple transistor cells at their output. These on-chip combining networks are a source of losses inherent to the power amplifier MMIC. By employing a differential configuration, on-chipcombining structures can be eliminated which leads to the reduction of losses. This enables the required output power for Direct Radiating Arrays using a simplified architecture with a better efficiency.This activity will investigate and develop transmit and receive differential front-end architectures for Ka-band direct radiating arrays. Trade-offs investigating different semiconductor technologies to realise differential MMIC amplifiers (power amplifier and low noise amplifier) will be performed. Critical breadboardingwill be undertaken to characterise the selected front-end architecture concept and the selected technology(ies). A full-scale engineering model of the selected implementation for a transmit and receive differential front-end in Ka-band will be manufactured and tested in relevant environment.

title: ARIEL - COOLER CONTROL ELECTRONICS (CCE) - RE-ISSUE
description: Ariel is the M4 mission in the Scientific Programme. It was adopted in November 2020 by the Science Programme Committee and is proceeding into the implementation phase, with the Spacecraft Prime contract to be kicked off by the end of 2021. Ariel will investigatethe atmospheres of many hundreds of diverse planets orbiting different types of stars to address fundamental scientific questions.Ariel is designed as a dedicated survey mission for transit and eclipse spectroscopy. Ariel observations require a specifically designed, stable payload and satellite platform with broad, instantaneous wavelength coverage extending from the visible to the infra-red (500 nm to 7.8 m). The detector technology selected to cover this wave range makes use of HgCdTe CMOS detectors. These detectors are optimised for astronomical observations, providing high Quantum Efficiency with low noise. As the cut-off wavelength of these detectors increase, these performance characteristic require operations in a colder environment. While the Ariel FGS instrument (500 nm to 1.95 m) can operate by making use of the passive cooling capabilities of the Ariel PLM (with the V-groove radiators), the AIRSinstrument (1.95 m to 7.8 m) requires further cooling down to 42 K with an active cryo-cooler. A Joule-Thomson (JT) cooler is therefore integrated in the system design and makes use of Neon as its working fluid (boiling point of 27.05 K at 1 atm). This cooler is developed by RAL (UK), under the responsibility of the UK Space Agency, within the AMC, as specified in the MLA, and builds on their experience from the Planck Helium JT cooler. This Ne JT Cooler is controlled by a warm electronic box, the CCE (Cooler Control Electronics), which is the subject of this procurement. While the cooler remains under the AMC's responsibility through UKSA and RAL(UK), the Agency, through the Ariel Project, has agreed to provide support to UKSA for the procurement of the CCE. Through this activity, the Contractor will be requested to provide the CCE, including development models as well as the Flight Model and spares. The due dates for these models range from 2022 to 2024, to secure the Ariel launch date. As well as providing the CCE unit, the contractwill cover the position sensor board, which interfaces to the CCE unit on the compressor. The contract will cover the full design and development of this CCE in line with the Ariel requirements.
